name: Rhizodus
fact: One of the largest freshwater fish that ever lived: a lobe-finned hunter up to about 7 m long, with fangs as long as a banana, in the rivers and swamps of the early Carboniferous. Lobe-finned fish are the group that land animals came from.

name: Meganeura
fact: One of the largest insects ever: a griffinfly, a relative of dragonflies, with wings as wide as a seagull’s. It hunted other insects in flight. Why insects could grow so big then is argued over: more oxygen in the air may have helped, and so may the lack of flying hunters — birds had not yet evolved.

name: Arthropleura
fact: A millipede relative as long as a small car — the largest arthropod that ever lived on land. It probably ate plants and rotting matter; exactly what is not known.
know: The largest arthropod that ever lived — a millipede relative up to 2.6 m long. For over 150 years no head had been found; in 2024, CT scans of juveniles from France finally showed one, with stalked eyes.

name: Hylonomus
fact: One of the oldest known reptiles, about 312 million years old, found inside the hollow stumps of fossil trees at Joggins in Nova Scotia. It looked like a small lizard. Reptiles, birds and mammals all come from animals that laid eggs on land; Hylonomus is among the oldest on the reptile side of that family.

name: Eryops
fact: A big amphibian built like a flat, stocky crocodile, up to about 2 m long, and one of the top hunters of its swamps. Like frogs today, it probably had to return to water to lay its eggs.

name: Pulmonate Snail
fact: Among the oldest land snails known: tiny shells found at Joggins in Nova Scotia, some inside hollow fossil tree stumps. They breathed air, like garden snails today.

name: Lepidodendron
fact: A scale tree: a giant relative of today’s little club mosses, up to 30 m tall, its trunk covered in a diamond pattern of leaf scars. Its swamp forests made much of the world’s coal. One idea was that wood could not rot then because fungi had not yet learned to break it down; later work argued that wet, sinking ground explains the coal better, and the question is still discussed.

name: Westlothiana
fact: Nicknamed “Lizzie”, it was hailed as the oldest reptile when it was found in Scotland in the 1980s. Study of its bones now puts it just outside the amniotes — close to the animals that lay eggs on land, but not yet one of them.

name: Edops
fact: A big, broad-headed amphibian, up to about 2 m long, with powerful jaws: a hunter at the water’s edge, a little like a giant salamander.

name: Petrolacosaurus
fact: One of the oldest known diapsids — reptiles with two openings in the skull behind each eye, the group that includes lizards, snakes, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds. It was not their ancestor but an early relative on a side branch: slender, long-legged and lizard-like.

name: Sigillaria
fact: A giant club-moss tree, cousin of Lepidodendron, with its leaf scars in straight rows up the trunk and a tuft of long, narrow leaves at the top. It grew in the coal swamps, including their drier parts.

name: Pulmonoscorpius
fact: A scorpion the length of a cat, from the oxygen-rich air of the Carboniferous. It breathed through book lungs, like scorpions today.

name: Tullimonstrum (Tully monster)
fact: Illinois's state fossil: eyes on a stiff crossbar and a long trunk ending in a toothed claw. Found by amateur collector Francis Tully in 1958.
debate: Nobody agrees what it was. A fish? A worm? A mollusc? Studies in 2016 and 2023 reached opposite conclusions.

name: Pederpes
fact: The first four-legged animal with feet that pointed forward for walking. It fills part of “Romer's gap”, a stretch of time once almost empty of land-animal fossils.

name: Crassigyrinus
fact: An eel-like water predator with tiny legs and huge jaws full of fangs — four legs did not mean leaving the water.

name: Falcatus
fact: A small shark relative. The males carried a long spine sweeping forward over the head — probably for display or courtship.

name: Archaeothyris
fact: One of the oldest known synapsids — the branch of the family tree that leads to mammals. It looked like a lizard but was on your side of the split.

name: Calamites
fact: A horsetail the size of a tree. Its relatives today grow knee-high in ditches.

name: Megarachne
fact: Described in 1980 as the largest spider ever. A second fossil found in 2005 showed it was a sea scorpion with a broad head — the giant spider never existed.

name: Akmonistion
fact: An “anvil shark”: in males, the fin on its back was a flat-topped brush covered in teeth-like scales, like a hairbrush on its back.

name: Edestus
fact: A shark relative with curved blades of teeth in both jaws that met like the blades of scissors.

name: Bandringa
fact: A shark with a long snout like a paddlefish. Young ones lived in swampy nurseries close to shore, then moved out to sea as adults (2014).

name: Mazothairos
fact: A giant insect with six wings — a small extra pair behind its head — and a beak for sucking plant juices.

name: Euphoberia
fact: A millipede covered in long forked spines, probably to put off predators.

name: Dendrerpeton
fact: An amphibian found, with early reptiles, inside the hollow stumps of fossil trees at Joggins — trapped where the trunks had rotted out.

name: Ophiderpeton
fact: A legless, snake-like amphibian — over 200 vertebrae and no limbs at all. Real snakes would not appear for another 150 million years.

name: Proterogyrinus
fact: A heavy-headed water predator with stout legs, related to the ancestors of reptiles.

name: Spinoaequalis
fact: A small reptile with a flattened, paddle-like tail — the first reptile known to have gone back to the water. Reptiles kept doing this for 300 million years.

name: Medullosa
fact: It looks like a fern but made seeds — some the size of hen's eggs. Seed ferns were among the first plants to make seeds.
